Whether a key can leave the module depends on its CKA_EXTRACTABLE and CKA_SENSITIVE attributes and the module policy.

definition: An OpenSSL 3.x provider plugin from the Open Quantum Safe project that adds post-quantum and hybrid algorithms from the liboqs library, mainly for testing and experimentation. OpenSSL applications can use them once the provider is loaded and the application or OpenSSL configuration asks for the algorithm.
technicalNote: Loaded with OSSL_PROVIDER_load, the -provider option or openssl.cnf; TLS groups are then chosen with the usual OpenSSL group settings. On OpenSSL 3.5 and later, an algorithm that OpenSSL's own default provider already implements (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and the hybrids it ships) is not offered through oqsprovider, and the README strongly discourages using the standardized algorithm families through it. The project says the provider is meant for research and prototyping and does not recommend relying on it in production or to protect sensitive data; check its README for the OpenSSL and liboqs versions and algorithm names of the release you use.

definition: A community-maintained collection of cryptographic algorithm implementations in Rust, published as modular crates on crates.io. Emphasizes type safety, zero-dependency design, and no_std compatibility.
technicalNote: Key crates: aes, sha2, p256, x25519-dalek. PQC is emerging: pqcrypto crate wraps PQClean reference implementations. The aws-lc-rs crate provides FIPS-validated crypto via AWS-LC bindings. RustCrypto traits (digest::Digest, signature::Signer) define common interfaces across implementations.

definition: A software design pattern that decouples cryptographic algorithm selection from application business logic, so that algorithms can be changed with little or no change to application code. Supports PQC migration.
technicalNote: Five common patterns: (1) Provider Abstraction — use a provider interface such as JCA or OpenSSL providers. (2) Config-Driven Selection — algorithm name from YAML/env var. (3) Hybrid/Composite — run classical + PQC in parallel. (4) Algorithm Negotiation — TLS-style capability advertisement. (5) Feature Flags — gradual PQC rollout per service.

definition: Open Quantum Safe C library — the reference implementation hub for post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. Maintained by the Open Quantum Safe project and serves as the foundation for oqsprovider, oqs-go, liboqs-python, and other language bindings.
technicalNote: Supports the NIST PQC algorithms plus additional candidates (for example HQC, FrodoKEM, Classic McEliece), with the exact set depending on the release and build options. Provides portable C and optimized implementations on some platforms. Not FIPS-validated itself; the Open Quantum Safe project describes it as for prototyping and evaluation. For FIPS needs, check a CMVP certificate for the exact module.

definition: A collection of clean, standalone C implementations of the post-quantum schemes in the NIST post-quantum project, written to be easy to integrate into libraries such as liboqs and the Rust pqcrypto crate. The project is retired and archived as read-only.
technicalNote: PQClean's automatically checked requirements include valid C99, no dynamic memory allocation and no preprocessor conditionals other than header guards; its checks for branching on secret data and for access to secret memory locations are listed as not yet done. The README says the project is retired and archived, and points to the PQ Code Package projects (mlkem-native, mldsa-native, slhdsa-c) for maintained ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA code. liboqs still carries code that originated in PQClean. Treat it as a reference source, not a validated module.

definition: Amazon's open-source cryptographic library, forked from BoringSSL. Specific AWS-LC FIPS module versions have FIPS 140-3 validation certificates; the validated boundary is the module version on the certificate, not the whole library. The aws-lc-rs Rust crate provides safe bindings.
technicalNote: Check the NIST CMVP certificate for the module version, algorithms and operating environments it covers before claiming validated ML-KEM or ML-DSA. The aws-lc-rs crate is a drop-in replacement for the ring crate in many use cases. AWS uses AWS-LC in many of its services; this entry does not claim it covers all AWS TLS.

definition: The bootstrapping secret used to authenticate to a secrets manager — the root credential that unlocks all other credentials. Protecting Secret Zero is the foundational security challenge in any secrets management architecture.
technicalNote: Common Secret Zero approaches: (1) Cloud IAM role binding (instance identity). (2) Vault AppRole with RoleID + SecretID. (3) TPM-based attestation (most secure). (4) SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity. For PQC: the TLS channel carrying Secret Zero requires ML-KEM protection to prevent HNDL capture of all downstream secrets.

definition: Secrets generated on-demand with a short TTL and automatically revoked when the lease expires. Replaces long-lived static credentials with ephemeral ones that expire after the requesting workload is done.
technicalNote: HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets engines include: database (PostgreSQL, MySQL), AWS IAM, Azure AD, GCP service accounts, SSH OTP, PKI certificates. Each credential has a lease_id and lease_duration. Renewing extends the TTL; revoking terminates early. PQC note: the lease signing key and TLS channel are the quantum-vulnerable components, not the dynamic credential itself.

definition: A secrets manager service that performs encryption/decryption operations on behalf of applications without ever exposing the key material. Acts as an 'encryption as a service' — applications send plaintext in, get ciphertext back.
technicalNote: HashiCorp Vault Transit engine supports AES-GCM-256, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA-OAEP, and ECDSA. Each named key has a versioned key ring — encrypting uses the latest version, decrypting accepts any version not older than the key's min_decryption_version setting. PQC migration depends on the key types the deployed Vault version documents; a KEM key type would establish a shared secret rather than encrypt data directly, and signature types such as ML-DSA only protect integrity. Rewrap re-encrypts existing ciphertext under the latest key version without exposing plaintext.

definition: The time-bounded validity period of a secret or token in a secrets manager. Every dynamically generated secret has a lease — it expires unless explicitly renewed before the TTL elapses.
technicalNote: Vault lease mechanics: lease_id identifies the secret, lease_duration is the TTL in seconds, renewable indicates whether renewal is allowed. Renewal resets the TTL up to the max_lease_ttl. Automated renewal via Vault Agent Sidecar or the Vault SDK. PQC note: the lease management API channel must be TLS with PQC hybrid KEX to prevent interception.

definition: The uncontrolled proliferation of secrets across an organization's systems — hardcoded in source code, scattered across config files, duplicated in environment variables, and stored in wikis or chat tools.
technicalNote: Common sprawl vectors: (1) .env files committed to git. (2) Secrets in CI/CD YAML. (3) Hardcoded in Dockerfiles or K8s manifests. (4) Exported to S3 / GCS buckets. (5) Shared via Slack or Confluence. Remediation: secret scanning tools (GitLeaks, TruffleHog, GitHub Secret Scanning) + secrets centralisation into a secrets manager. PQC relevance: sprawled secrets stored encrypted with RSA/AES-128 are HNDL targets.

definition: Bring Your Own Key — a cloud encryption model where the customer provides and manages the root encryption key rather than using a key generated and managed by the cloud provider. Gives customers control over key lifecycle and access.
technicalNote: BYOK implementations differ by provider. AWS KMS imports key material only under an RSA wrapping key (RSA_2048, RSA_3072 or RSA_4096) and cannot import key material into ML-DSA or ML-KEM KMS keys. Azure Key Vault BYOK transfers a key wrapped with CKM_RSA_AES_KEY_WRAP under an RSA-HSM key exchange key of 2048, 3072 or 4096 bits. Google Cloud KMS key import wraps key material for transfer, with RSA-based import methods alongside the quantum-safe HPKE methods. Where the wrap is RSA, it is the PQC-vulnerable step of BYOK; ML-KEM is not an import wrapping option for AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault. Post-import, the customer key wraps DEKs using AES-256 which is quantum-safe.

definition: A two-level encryption scheme: a data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the data, and a key encryption key (KEK) encrypts the DEK. The encrypted DEK is stored alongside the ciphertext. Only the KEK needs to be protected in a KMS.
technicalNote: Used by AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and Google Cloud KMS, each of which documents this pattern. PQC migration: the quantum-vulnerable step is the KEK wrapping operation when it uses RSA-OAEP or ECDH; the AES-256-GCM DEK is not itself exposed to Shor-type attacks. An ML-KEM-768 encapsulation yields a shared secret; a KDF bound to the algorithm and context derives a KEK that authenticated-wraps the DEK. A hybrid design mixes the classical and KEM secrets in that KDF, so the KEK stays secret as long as at least one of the two secrets does, provided the combiner is sound. Wrapping the same DEK separately under a classical KEK and a post-quantum KEK keeps classical-only readers working, but the DEK is then only as protected as the weaker wrap, because opening either copy recovers it. Wrapped DEKs already captured under the old wrap stay exposed.

definition: A dedicated service for storing, rotating, and auditing application secrets such as database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, and SSH keys. Provides centralized access control, automatic rotation, and audit logging.
technicalNote: Key products: HashiCorp Vault (open source + enterprise), AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, Delinea Secret Server, CyberArk Conjur. Core capabilities: versioning, rotation triggers (AWS Lambda), access policies (IAM or Vault policies), audit logs, replication. PQC considerations: hybrid key exchange on the TLS connection to a secrets API needs both the service endpoint and the client to support it (AWS lists hybrid post-quantum key exchange as launched on Secrets Manager's FIPS and non-FIPS endpoints in commercial and US GovCloud Regions, which clients must be updated to offer). Signing algorithms are product-specific; Vault's documented identity-token algorithms are RS256/384/512, ES256/384/512 and EdDSA, with no post-quantum option listed.

definition: A network traffic analysis technique that examines packet payloads (not just headers) to classify, filter, or log traffic. Used by firewalls, IDS/IPS, and network monitoring tools to enforce security policies.
technicalNote: PQC impact on DPI: ML-KEM-768 hybrid key exchanges produce significantly larger TLS ClientHello messages (2–4× increase). ML-DSA certificates are 2–5× larger than ECDSA. Many inline DPI appliances have fixed packet buffer sizes that will need firmware/hardware upgrades. Network taps must accommodate increased session state for hybrid key exchanges.

definition: A network security technique where a proxy or firewall decrypts, inspects, and re-encrypts TLS traffic inline. Also called SSL/TLS interception or man-in-the-middle inspection. Used for DLP, malware scanning, and policy enforcement.
technicalNote: PQC can affect TLS inspection designs: (1) a proxy that terminates both legs may negotiate different groups on each leg, so check which hybrid groups each leg supports and whether the proxy re-encrypts onward; (2) PQC certificate chains and key shares are larger, which can affect devices with fixed buffers or hardware offload; (3) per-connection overhead depends on the implementation. Check each vendor's documentation for the product, version and configuration that supports this.

definition: Next-Generation Firewall — a stateful network firewall that integrates application-layer inspection, user identity awareness, TLS inspection, IDS/IPS, and threat intelligence. Replaces traditional port-based packet filters with application-aware policies.
technicalNote: PQC support varies by vendor, product, version and configuration; check each vendor's release notes rather than assuming a timeline. Inline PQC at line rate may need hardware capacity that older appliances lack, so confirm with the vendor.

definition: Intrusion Detection System / Intrusion Prevention System — network security tools that monitor traffic for known attack patterns (signature-based) or anomalous behaviour (anomaly-based). IPS operates inline and can block traffic; IDS is passive.
technicalNote: PQC impact on IDS/IPS: (1) Signature updates may be needed for PQC-protocol-aware rules (detecting ML-KEM TLS extensions, PQC certificate OIDs). (2) Anomaly baselines may need recalibration because PQC increases normal traffic sizes, which can trigger false positives on size-based rules. (3) Encrypted traffic analysis tools cannot inspect ML-KEM sessions without a TLS inspection proxy. Check each product's documentation for protocol-parser support.

definition: A security model that grants access to specific applications based on verified identity, device posture, and context — rather than network location. Replaces implicit trust based on being inside the corporate network perimeter.
technicalNote: ZTNA PQC design points to check, not universal requirements: (1) mutual TLS device authentication with post-quantum or hybrid certificates once your PKI and clients support them; (2) hybrid ML-KEM key exchange in the secure tunnel; (3) device attestation via TPM Quote or DICE (see attestation PQC migration); (4) identity tokens signed with a post-quantum algorithm such as ML-DSA, whose JOSE identifiers are registered in RFC 9964, once your identity provider and relying parties support it. Support varies by vendor and product; confirm each point in the vendor's own documentation.

definition: Terminating TLS connections at a dedicated hardware appliance or load balancer, rather than at the application server. Reduces CPU load on application servers and centralises certificate management.
technicalNote: PQC impact on TLS offload: ML-DSA-65 operations require ~3× more compute than ECDSA P-256 per operation. ML-KEM-768 key exchange is ~5× the data size of X25519. Hardware SSL accelerators (Intel QAT, Marvell NITROX, Broadcom BCM585xx) will require firmware/hardware refresh for PQC-accelerated operations. Software offload (HAProxy, nginx, Envoy) can be patched to support hybrid TLS via OQS-OpenSSL.

definition: Network traffic that flows laterally between servers, containers, or services within a data centre or cloud environment — as opposed to north-south traffic which flows between users and services across the network perimeter.
technicalNote: East-west PQC considerations: service meshes such as Istio and Linkerd issue short-lived workload certificates, 24 hours by default in their documentation, and rotate them automatically. A short lifetime limits how long a stolen private key can be used to impersonate a workload; it does not protect the confidentiality of recorded traffic, which depends on the key exchange negotiated in each TLS handshake (Istio lets operators set the ECDH curves). Authentication moves to post-quantum certificates only when the mesh CA, proxies and any SPIFFE/SPIRE components support them; check each project's current documentation.

definition: A network security technique that creates fine-grained security zones within a data centre, isolating individual workloads or applications from each other. Limits blast radius when an attacker gains access to one segment.
technicalNote: Micro-segmentation policy enforcement relies on workload identity (via TLS certificates or hardware attestation). PQC migration may involve: (1) policy engine certificates moving to post-quantum or hybrid certificates; (2) workload identity tokens using post-quantum signatures; (3) policy distribution channels using hybrid TLS. Agent and controller support varies by product; confirm it in the vendor's documentation.

definition: A database encryption feature that automatically encrypts data files at rest without requiring application changes. The database engine handles encryption and decryption transparently on read/write operations.
technicalNote: TDE implementations: SQL Server encrypts data and log files with a symmetric database encryption key (AES or 3DES) protected by a certificate or an EKM-held asymmetric key; Oracle protects its table and tablespace keys with a master encryption key kept in a TDE wallet or an external keystore such as Oracle Key Vault; core PostgreSQL has no TDE (its documentation points to pgcrypto for columns and to file-system or block-level encryption), and Percona's pg_tde adds it but ships with Percona Server for PostgreSQL and requires that distribution's patches. Which key protects the data-encryption key depends on the product's key provider, so inspect that provider. PQC note: a KEM such as ML-KEM establishes a shared secret; protecting a master key with it needs a KDF and key-wrap profile that the product and key provider document.

definition: Database encryption applied to individual columns rather than the entire database or table. Allows selective protection of sensitive fields (SSN, credit card, health records) while leaving non-sensitive data unencrypted and queryable.
technicalNote: SQL Server Always Encrypted uses two keys: Column Master Key (CMK, stored in Key Vault or certificate store) + Column Encryption Key (CEK, stored in database metadata, encrypted by CMK). Oracle TDE column encryption uses similar hierarchy. PostgreSQL pgcrypto provides column encryption via SQL functions. PQC note: an RSA-protected CMK is the quantum-vulnerable step. A KEM alone does not wrap keys; migration needs a key provider and client driver that document a PQC-capable KEM, KDF and key-wrap profile.

definition: Microsoft SQL Server's client-side encryption feature: a client driver encrypts sensitive columns before they reach the database engine, and the encryption keys stay in an external key store rather than in the database. Without secure enclaves the engine handles only ciphertext. With secure enclaves, the client driver passes keys to a protected memory region inside the engine process, which decrypts there to allow richer queries.
technicalNote: Always Encrypted uses a two-tier key hierarchy: the Column Master Key (CMK, held in an external key store) protects Column Encryption Keys (AES-256). Microsoft's CMK store providers encrypt CEKs with RSA-OAEP; a custom provider may differ. Without enclaves, deterministic encryption supports equality lookups and randomised encryption supports only storing and retrieving values. With secure enclaves, randomised columns also support comparisons, pattern matching and in-place encryption; this needs enclave-enabled keys, with the CMK held in the Windows Certificate Store or Azure Key Vault, and Microsoft notes that such columns can leak the order of the data. A PQC migration is hypothetical until Microsoft and the key store provider document a supported scheme; do not assume a rotation wizard or client driver supports it.

definition: An encryption scheme that allows a database server to execute certain queries over encrypted data without decrypting it first. MongoDB's Queryable Encryption encrypts fields on the client and supports equality queries, and in newer releases range queries, over encrypted indexes. It is different from storage encryption such as TDE, which the server decrypts transparently.
technicalNote: MongoDB documents client-side encryption of the fields, with AES and HMAC-SHA-256 primitives; check its protocol documentation for how query tokens are produced and for the leakage profile (access patterns can still reveal information). This entry asserts no PQC roadmap for it.

definition: Hold Your Own Key — a cloud encryption model where the customer holds a key that never leaves their on-premises HSM. The cloud service requests encryption operations from the customer HSM rather than using cloud-side keys.
technicalNote: HYOK implementations: Azure Information Protection HYOK (AD RMS key on-prem), Google Workspace Client-Side Encryption (CSE). Contrast with BYOK: in BYOK the customer imports the key into the cloud KMS; in HYOK the key never leaves the customer HSM. PQC migration: the HSM must support ML-KEM for key wrapping and ML-DSA for signing before HYOK's quantum safety can be claimed.

definition: A symmetric key used to directly encrypt data. In envelope encryption architectures, the DEK is a short-lived, per-object AES key that encrypts actual data, while a Key Encryption Key (KEK) protects the DEK.
technicalNote: DEK sizing: AES-256 is the common choice for long-lived data confidentiality; its idealized Grover search cost is far beyond practical reach, though that is a model-dependent estimate rather than a guarantee. Rotation follows the documented cryptoperiod in the key-management policy (see NIST SP 800-57) and any applicable compliance requirement. PQC note: a DEK is only as protected as the key that wraps it. If the KEK or wrapping step uses RSA or ECDH, an adversary who captured the wrapped DEK and ciphertext can target the wrap, not the AES key.

definition: The top-level key in SQL Server Always Encrypted that protects Column Encryption Keys (CEKs). The CMK is typically stored in Azure Key Vault, Windows Certificate Store, or an HSM — never in the database itself.
technicalNote: The CMK encrypts each CEK; the encrypted CEK values are stored as metadata in sys.column_encryption_key_values, while the CMK stays in the external key store. Rotating the CMK (the SSMS Rotate dialog, or the PowerShell cmdlets Invoke-SqlColumnMasterKeyRotation and Complete-SqlColumnMasterKeyRotation) re-encrypts every CEK under the new CMK without touching column data, and Microsoft advises keeping the old CMK because earlier backups still need it. Because the CEK itself is unchanged, an old wrapped copy stays tied to the old RSA key; replacing the CEK means re-encrypting the column data. A PQC migration is hypothetical until the key provider and client driver document a PQC-capable scheme; a KEM only establishes a shared secret, so such a scheme would also need a KDF to derive a key-encryption key and an authenticated wrap of the CEK, with algorithm and context bound in and the key version recorded.

definition: The process of replacing an active database encryption key with a new one, re-encrypting data (or key metadata) under the new key, and retiring the old key. Critical for limiting cryptographic exposure over time.
technicalNote: Three rotation strategies: (1) Master key rotation only — re-encrypt DEKs/CEKs under a new master key without touching data. (2) DEK rotation — generate a new DEK and re-encrypt all data (expensive). (3) Combined — a new master key and new DEKs. SQL Server and Oracle each offer both kinds of rotation, and earlier master key versions are kept so older backups can be restored. A PQC migration of the master-key layer would be strategy (1) where the product and key provider document a supported scheme: the KEM shared secret goes through a KDF to a key-encryption key that authenticated-wraps the DEK, with context bound in and the key version stored with it. Rewrapping does not protect copies of the old wrapped DEK and ciphertext already captured, including backups; that needs DEK replacement and data re-encryption.

definition: A system that creates, maintains, and manages digital identities and their authentication. The IdP authenticates users and issues tokens (SAML assertions, JWT, OIDC ID tokens) that allow access to service providers.
technicalNote: PQC impact on IdPs: (1) SAML assertion signatures — migrate from RSA-SHA256 to a post-quantum signature once supported. (2) OIDC/JWT signing — migrate from RS256/ES256 to ML-DSA-65, whose JOSE identifier is registered in RFC 9964, once your libraries and relying parties support it. (3) TLS channel to IdP — hybrid ML-KEM. (4) PKI certificates for IdP servers — ML-DSA-65 or hybrid. Examples of IdPs: Okta, Microsoft Entra, PingFederate, Shibboleth. Ask each vendor for its documented PQC support; this entry asserts no roadmap.

definition: In federated identity, the system that provides a service or resource and relies on an Identity Provider to authenticate users. The SP trusts the IdP and validates tokens presented by users.
technicalNote: SP-IdP trust: in SAML, the SP stores the IdP public key/certificate for assertion verification — this is the RSA/ECDSA-vulnerable point. In OIDC, the SP fetches the IdP JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) at runtime for JWT verification. PQC migration: IdP must update its signing key to ML-DSA-65 and advertise it in the JWKS endpoint. SPs need updated JWT libraries that support ML-DSA verification.

definition: Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 — an XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between identity providers and service providers. The dominant enterprise SSO federation protocol.
technicalNote: SAML assertions are XML documents that can be signed with XML Signature (xmldsig), for example with RSA-SHA256. The PQC migration challenge: check whether the XML Signature specification and your SAML libraries define identifiers for post-quantum signatures. One design discussed is wrapping the assertion in a JWS signed with a post-quantum algorithm; that is not a SAML interoperability standard and would need library support on both sides, although ML-DSA identifiers for JOSE are now registered (RFC 9964). This entry assumes no SAML 3.0 specification.

definition: OpenID Connect — an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that allows clients to verify user identity based on authentication performed by an authorization server. Issues ID tokens (JWTs) containing user identity claims.
technicalNote: OIDC PQC migration: JWTs are signed using JOSE algorithms (RS256, ES256, EdDSA). JOSE PQC draft (IETF draft-ietf-jose-pqc-signatures) adds ML-DSA-44/65/87 as alg values. ID tokens signed with ML-DSA-65 are ~3KB vs ~1KB for RS256 — HTTP header size limits may need adjustment. OIDC discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) JWKS endpoint must expose ML-DSA public keys.

definition: A network authentication protocol that uses symmetric key cryptography and a trusted third party (Key Distribution Center) to authenticate service requests. The dominant authentication protocol in Microsoft Active Directory environments.
technicalNote: Kerberos PQC challenges: (1) Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) and Service Tickets are encrypted with symmetric keys whose encryption type depends on what the client, KDC and service have enabled; AES-256 types are defined (RFC 3962, RFC 8009), and a 256-bit key's quantum resistance depends on the attack model, not the label. (2) Pre-authentication uses AS-REQ with the client long-term key; certificate-based PKINIT (RFC 4556) is the existing option, and whether a given KDC supports post-quantum certificates must be confirmed with the vendor. (3) Cross-realm trust uses shared symmetric keys. This entry asserts no vendor release date.

definition: A security model based on the principle of 'never trust, always verify' — no implicit trust is granted based on network location. Every access request must be authenticated, authorized, and continuously validated regardless of origin.
technicalNote: NIST SP 800-207 defines ZTA principles. Core pillars: Identity (ML-DSA certificates), Device (TPM attestation with PQC), Network (micro-segmentation with ML-DSA-signed policies), Application (mutual TLS with PQC certificates), Data (encryption with ML-KEM-protected keys). ZTA PQC dependency chain: identity proofing → ML-DSA credential issuance → PQC-secured policy engine → ML-KEM-protected data.

definition: The process of cryptographically proving a device's identity and integrity to a remote verifier. Allows a server to verify that a device is what it claims to be and that its firmware/software has not been tampered with.
technicalNote: Attestation mechanisms: TPM 2.0 Quote (RSA/ECDSA AIK signs PCR measurements — quantum-vulnerable), DICE, FIDO Device Onboarding, Intel TDX quotes (ECDSA P-256 in Intel's DCAP quote format) and AMD SEV-SNP attestation reports (ECDSA P-384 with SHA-384). Post-quantum support in these ecosystems varies; check each specification and vendor for what is published. IAM systems increasingly require device attestation for Zero Trust.

definition: An identity trust relationship between two or more organizations that allows users from one organization to authenticate with another's services using their home organization's credentials. Enables SSO across organizational boundaries.
technicalNote: Federation protocols: SAML 2.0 (XML-based, enterprise), OIDC (JSON-based, modern web), WS-Federation (Microsoft legacy). Federation trust anchors: SAML metadata signing certificates (RSA-2048/ECDSA, 3-year TTL typical). PQC migration: federation metadata must be re-signed with ML-DSA-65 certificates, and metadata signing certificates published via HTTPS with ML-DSA-secured TLS. eduGAIN, InCommon, and Azure AD B2B federation are high-priority PQC migration targets.

definition: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface — the modern replacement for BIOS that defines a software interface between an operating system and platform firmware. UEFI Secure Boot uses a cryptographic chain of trust to verify firmware and bootloader integrity.
technicalNote: UEFI Secure Boot key hierarchy: Platform Key (PK) → Key Exchange Keys (KEK) → Signature Databases (db/dbx). Entries can be X.509 certificates, RSA-2048 public keys or image hashes. PQC migration: the UEFI Forum's April 2026 whitepaper describes post-quantum changes for the next UEFI specification release, including support for images that carry more than one signature, and states that these proposals are not yet approved. Check the published specification and the firmware vendor for what a given platform supports.

definition: The root of trust in UEFI Secure Boot: a single key whose private half the platform owner uses to change platform ownership and to authorise changes to the Key Exchange Key (KEK) list. The platform vendor can supply a default Platform Key, and the platform owner enrolls their own.
technicalNote: PK characteristics: only one PK at a time (the PK variable holds exactly one entry); in user mode a new PK must be signed with the current PK, and the PK can also be cleared by a secure platform-specific method. RSA-2048 is widely used today. PQC: the UEFI Forum's April 2026 whitepaper proposes changes for the next UEFI release and states that they are not yet approved, so no migration path is published. Microsoft Shim and MOK (Machine Owner Key) system for Linux adds another trust layer.

definition: A UEFI Secure Boot key that is trusted to update the Signature Database (db) and Revocation Database (dbx). Updates to the KEK list itself must be signed by the Platform Key (PK), and the KEK lets OS vendors add their own signing certificates to the Secure Boot databases.
technicalNote: KEK signers: Microsoft holds a KEK that allows updating the Windows db; OEM holds another KEK. Multiple KEKs can coexist. KEK updates require a valid PK signature. PQC: the UEFI Forum's April 2026 whitepaper describes planned post-quantum changes for the next UEFI release, including an algorithm check when PK, KEK, db or dbx entries are enrolled, and states that its proposals are not yet approved; check the published specification and the firmware vendor before planning a migration.

definition: Device Identifier Composition Engine — a hardware security architecture that uses a secret Unique Device Secret (UDS) and firmware measurement to derive a Compound Device Identifier (CDI), creating a hardware root of trust that is unique per device and firmware state.
technicalNote: DICE layers: DICE layer 0 (hardware) derives the CDI from the UDS and a measurement of the first mutable code; the TCG specification allows a hash or an HMAC, HMAC(UDS, H(First Mutable Code)), and leaves the method to the manufacturer. Each subsequent layer generates a key pair from its CDI and issues a certificate binding the key to a firmware measurement. Algorithms are chosen by profiles: the Open Profile for DICE v2.6 lists ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 as acceptable post-quantum signatures, and the Android profile for DICE accepts the same two.

definition: Platform Configuration Register — a hash accumulator inside a TPM that holds extended measurements of system components. PCRs cannot be written directly; they can only be extended (PCR_new = SHA-256(PCR_old || new_value)), creating a tamper-evident log of the boot process.
technicalNote: Typical PC firmware assignments (TCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile): PCR[0] = SRTM, BIOS and embedded drivers, PCR[4] = UEFI boot manager code, PCR[7] = Secure Boot policy; PCRs 8-15 are left to the operating system. A PCR holds a digest, never a key. Extend uses the PCR bank's hash (for example SHA-256); the quantum-vulnerable operation is the TPM Quote, where an attestation key signs PCR values with RSA or ECDSA. TPM 2.0 library version 185 defines ML-DSA attestation keys; check the manufacturer's documentation for whether a given TPM implements them.

definition: A boot integrity mechanism where each stage of the boot process measures (hashes) the next stage and extends the measurement into TPM PCRs. Unlike Secure Boot which enforces policy by blocking unsigned code, Measured Boot records what ran for later attestation.
technicalNote: Measured Boot phases: UEFI firmware → PCR[0]; Secure Boot variables → PCR[7]; bootloader → PCR[4]; OS kernel → PCR[8–10]. The PCR log (TCG Event Log) records what was measured. Remote attestation uses PCR values + event log. PQC note: SHA-256 PCR extend is quantum-safe; only the attestation quote signature requires PQC migration.

definition: The process of cryptographically signing firmware images before distribution and verifying the signature before execution. Ensures that firmware has not been tampered with since it was signed by the vendor.
technicalNote: Firmware signing formats: UEFI authenticated variables and images (PKCS#7 SignedData with X.509 certificates, commonly RSA-2048 or ECDSA), FIT (Flat Image Tree for embedded/ARM). PQC migration: an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309 bytes (an RSA-2048 signature is 256 bytes), so check size limits in firmware variables and update formats. Images that carry both a classical and an ML-DSA signature are a transition approach discussed in a UEFI Forum whitepaper, not a published UEFI requirement. UEFI capsule updates are one common firmware update mechanism.

definition: Intel's boot integrity technology: hardware-based verification of the initial BIOS startup code before it runs, according to a boot policy defined by the platform manufacturer. It is intended to help prevent the execution of unauthorized boot blocks.
technicalNote: The platform manufacturer chooses the boot policy: an enforcement policy (what happens if the BIOS cannot be verified) and a measurement policy (whether the BIOS startup code is measured into the TPM). Intel's datasheet pages for this technology do not state the signature algorithms or key sizes used, and this entry makes no claim about them or about post-quantum support; check the platform documentation for your processor. Availability varies between processor SKUs.

definition: A system-wide configuration that sets the default cryptographic algorithm preferences for all supported applications and libraries. Red Hat-based systems use update-crypto-policies; Debian-based systems configure algorithm preferences via OpenSSL and GnuTLS configuration files.
technicalNote: Red Hat crypto-policies (RHEL 8+): update-crypto-policies --set FUTURE disables SHA-1 and RSA-2048. A custom PQC policy flows to OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, Kerberos, and Java via /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ symlinks. Create a PQC policy: echo '[alg_policy] cipher = AES-256-GCM hybrid-ml-kem' > /etc/crypto-policies/policies/PQC.pol; update-crypto-policies --set PQC.

definition: Microsoft's Secure Channel cryptographic package — the TLS/SSL implementation built into Windows. SChannel is used by IIS, WinHTTP, and most Windows network services. It uses CNG (Cryptography API: Next Generation) for algorithm implementations.
technicalNote: SChannel PQC support: check Microsoft's current CNG and SChannel documentation for which Windows versions support ML-KEM hybrid key exchange and ML-DSA, and for the exact configuration (registry keys or Group Policy). This entry asserts no version, registry path or release date.

definition: A long-term asymmetric key pair used to authenticate an SSH server to connecting clients. When a client connects for the first time, it receives and stores the server's host key fingerprint in known_hosts. Future connections verify against this stored fingerprint.
technicalNote: SSH host key algorithms: RSA (rsa-sha2-512), ECDSA P-256 (ecdsa-sha2-nistp256), Ed25519. OpenSSH's post-quantum key exchange came first (sntrup761x25519-sha512 default from 9.0; mlkem768x25519-sha256 added in 9.9 and default from 10.0); it protects session keys, not host-key authentication. For host keys, OpenSSH 10.4 added an experimental composite of ML-DSA-44 and Ed25519 (ssh-mldsa44-ed25519, not enabled by default), specified in an individual Internet-Draft, and 10.6 enables it: its sshd_config(5) lists ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 among the default host key algorithms. Both client and server need a version that supports it. Post-quantum signatures are typically much larger than Ed25519's 64-byte signature, depending on the algorithm and parameter set.

definition: An operating-system setting that restricts cryptographic operations to the algorithms and settings permitted under FIPS 140. FIPS 140-3 validates cryptographic modules, not settings, so a system uses validated cryptography only if the modules it relies on hold a current validation certificate. U.S. federal agencies that require cryptographic protection must use validated modules.
technicalNote: FIPS 140-3 and PQC: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA are specified in FIPS 203/204/205, but a module's validation covers only the algorithms on its own certificate. For example, certificate #4282 (OpenSSL FIPS Provider 3.0.8 and 3.0.9) is a FIPS 140-2 certificate on the historical list with no ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA, while AWS-LC 3 certificates #5298 and #5314 are FIPS 140-3 and list ML-KEM. In the Linux crypto-policies framework the FIPS policy aids conformance but does not provide it by itself: validated modules must be installed and the kernel booted with fips=1. Test applications before enforcing: the policy allows only TLS 1.2 and later.

definition: A configuration syntax used in GnuTLS to specify which TLS protocol versions, cipher suites, and key exchange algorithms are acceptable. Used in Linux systems as the TLS policy configuration for applications using the GnuTLS library.
technicalNote: GnuTLS priority examples: NORMAL means all the known-to-be-secure ciphersuites, and SECURE256 is currently an alias for SECURE192 (ciphersuites offering a 192-bit security level or more); a leading @ expands a keyword from the system-wide configuration. Post-quantum support depends on the GnuTLS release and its build: 3.8.8 (November 2024) added experimental X25519MLKEM768 and SecP256r1MLKEM768 key exchange, and from 3.8.10 (July 2025) post-quantum algorithms are provided only through a build with leancrypto. Check the GnuTLS documentation for the exact priority keywords before use. GnuTLS is one of several TLS libraries a program can be built with (curl, for example, can use GnuTLS, OpenSSL and others), so check which library a given program uses.

definition: A dynamically loadable module that extends OpenSSL with additional cryptographic algorithm implementations. In OpenSSL 3.x, all algorithm implementations are providers — the default provider supplies standard algorithms, and third-party providers (like oqsprovider) add PQC algorithms.
technicalNote: OpenSSL 3.5+ supplies ML-KEM and ML-DSA in its default provider; additional implementations may use third-party providers. Native OpenSSL 3.6 example, with sample-cert.pem and its matching sample-key.pem already prepared: openssl s_server -tls1_3 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -cert sample-cert.pem -key sample-key.pem. X25519MLKEM768 is one combined key-establishment group; a colon-separated list such as X25519:P-256 offers alternatives rather than combining them. Available groups depend on the build and providers. Check the negotiated group and cipher suite: library support alone does not establish that an application and its peer can negotiate a hybrid connection. Hybrid key establishment does not make the certificate PQC-signed. This native CLI example does not establish browser WASM command support. References: https://docs.openssl.org/3.6/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/ and https://docs.openssl.org/3.6/man1/openssl-s_server/.

definition: A systematic comparison of an organization's current cryptographic posture against regulatory requirements, identifying where PQC migration is needed to meet compliance deadlines. Evaluates frameworks like CNSA 2.0, DORA, NIS2, and sector-specific mandates across multiple jurisdictions.
technicalNote: A PQC compliance gap analysis typically covers: (1) algorithm inventory vs. approved algorithms, (2) certificate lifecycle vs. regulatory deadlines, (3) vendor PQC readiness vs. contractual obligations, (4) data retention periods vs. HNDL exposure windows. Multi-jurisdiction organizations must reconcile overlapping requirements.

definition: A measure of an organization's vulnerability to quantum computing threats, combining data sensitivity, cryptographic algorithm usage, data retention periods, and the estimated timeline to a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC).
technicalNote: Quantum risk exposure is typically assessed across four dimensions: Quantum Exposure (HNDL/HNFL window overlap), Migration Complexity (infrastructure depth and algorithm diversity), Regulatory Pressure (compliance deadline proximity), and Organizational Readiness (crypto-agility maturity and team capability).

definition: The legal obligation of corporate board members and executives to exercise due care in protecting organizational assets, including digital assets threatened by quantum computing. Failure to plan for known cryptographic risks may constitute a breach of fiduciary responsibility.

The estimated total cost of transitioning an organization's cryptographic infrastructure to post-quantum algorithms, including hardware upgrades, software updates, staff training, compliance certification, and operational overhead during the hybrid transition period.
technicalNote: Key cost drivers: HSM firmware upgrades ($50K–$500K per cluster), certificate re-issuance across PKI hierarchy, application code changes for larger key/signature sizes, re-certification costs (FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria), and potential performance infrastructure upgrades to handle increased computational and bandwidth requirements.

definition: The significant increase in cryptographic key and signature sizes when migrating from classical to post-quantum algorithms. ML-KEM public keys are 800–1568 bytes (vs. 32–91 for ECC), and ML-DSA signatures are 2420–4627 bytes (vs. 64–72 for ECDSA), affecting APIs, protocols, and storage.
technicalNote: Practical impacts: JWT tokens may exceed HTTP header limits, TLS handshakes require additional round trips, certificate chains grow 10–50x, PKCS#11 buffer sizes need adjustment, and database column widths for stored keys must be expanded. Performance budgets for latency-sensitive applications (payments, IoT) require careful re-evaluation.

definition: The ability of network intermediary devices (firewalls, load balancers, DPI appliances, TLS inspection proxies) to correctly process PQC-sized TLS handshakes and certificates without dropping, truncating, or rejecting connections due to unexpected packet sizes.
technicalNote: ML-KEM-768 adds ~1100 bytes to TLS ClientHello; some middleboxes with hardcoded buffer limits will drop oversized handshakes. Testing strategy: deploy hybrid TLS (X25519+ML-KEM-768) in monitoring mode before enforcement, use QUIC where possible to avoid TCP middlebox issues, and coordinate with network security vendors on firmware updates.

definition: The accumulated technical risk from hardcoded algorithm choices, missing abstraction layers, and tight coupling between application logic and specific cryptographic implementations, making PQC migration more difficult and costly.
technicalNote: Common sources: hardcoded "RSA-2048" strings in config files, direct OpenSSL API calls without provider abstraction, fixed-size key buffers, algorithm-specific serialization formats, and certificate templates that assume specific key types. Crypto-agile architecture eliminates this debt by design.

definition: The allocation of computational resources (CPU cycles, memory, bandwidth, latency) for cryptographic operations within an application or system. PQC algorithms have different performance profiles than classical algorithms, requiring budget redesign during migration.
technicalNote: ML-KEM-768 encapsulation is ~5x faster than ECDH P-256 but produces larger ciphertexts. ML-DSA-65 signing is comparable to Ed25519 but verification is slower and signatures are ~36x larger. SLH-DSA is orders of magnitude slower for signing but provides hash-based security without lattice assumptions. Architecture decisions must balance security level, performance, and bandwidth constraints per use case.

definition: The coordinated process of upgrading cryptographic configurations across an entire fleet of servers, endpoints, IoT devices, and network appliances to support post-quantum algorithms, typically executed in phased rollouts with rollback capability.
technicalNote: Fleet migration phases: (1) inventory and dependency mapping, (2) canary deployment to 1–5% of fleet, (3) staged rollout with health checks, (4) enforcement with monitoring, (5) legacy algorithm sunset. Configuration management tools (Ansible, Terraform, Chef) must be updated to manage PQC-specific parameters like hybrid key exchange groups and larger certificate chains.

definition: The operational challenge of replacing certificates across large infrastructure deployments when migrating to PQC algorithms, complicated by larger certificate sizes, new CA hierarchies, and the need to maintain backward compatibility during the transition period.
technicalNote: Key considerations: ACME/cert-manager automation must support PQC certificate types, multi-CA coordination when different CAs adopt PQC at different rates, certificate transparency (CT) log compatibility with larger PQC certificates, and monitoring for mixed classical/PQC certificate environments. Expect 10–50x increase in certificate chain sizes affecting TLS handshake latency.

definition: Research datasets, publications, and intellectual property that require long-term confidentiality (20–50+ years) and integrity protection, making them particularly vulnerable to Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks and requiring early PQC adoption.
technicalNote: High-risk research domains: genomics and bioinformatics (patient privacy regulations extend decades), classified defense research (50+ year confidentiality), pharmaceutical R&D (patent-sensitive data during 20-year exclusivity periods), and financial modeling (proprietary algorithms with long competitive value). Research institutions should prioritize encrypting data at rest with hybrid PQC schemes.

definition: Mathematical proof techniques used to verify that cryptographic algorithm implementations correctly conform to their specifications, providing stronger assurance than testing alone. Critical for PQC algorithms where implementation subtleties can introduce vulnerabilities.
technicalNote: Active PQC formal verification efforts: NIST PQC standards are being verified using tools like EasyCrypt, Jasmin, and CryptoVerif. Lattice-based schemes require careful verification of polynomial arithmetic and sampling. Side-channel resistance claims also benefit from formal verification of constant-time implementation properties.

definition: A network analysis technique that inspects encrypted traffic in-flight without injecting any packets. Used to detect and classify cryptographic algorithms across TLS, SSH, IKEv2, and OT protocols by analyzing observable handshake metadata on a SPAN port or network tap.
technicalNote: Tools like CryptoNext COMPASS and pqc-flow operate in passive mode — zero packets are injected, making them safe for production environments including OT/ICS. Observable data includes ClientHello cipher suites, server certificate algorithms, key exchange group identifiers, and SSH algorithm negotiation. Cannot validate whether a remote endpoint actively supports PQC — only detects what is being used in current flows.

definition: A network assessment technique that initiates real connections to target endpoints to probe which cryptographic algorithms they support. Unlike passive discovery, active scanning actively negotiates TLS/SSH/IKEv2 handshakes to discover PQC readiness.
technicalNote: Tools like pqcscan (Anvil Secure, Rust-based) and SSLyze probe endpoints by attempting handshakes with specific algorithm sets. Key metrics collected: supported PQC algorithms, hybrid key exchange groups, TLS versions, certificate details, and risk scores. Active scanning requires network access and generates detectable connection attempts — should be coordinated with security operations before running at scale.

definition: A statistical methodology for detecting side-channel information leakage in cryptographic hardware implementations. Uses Welch's t-test to determine whether power consumption during cryptographic operations is statistically correlated with secret key data.
technicalNote: TVLA has a non-specific fixed-vs-random test and specific tests on chosen intermediate values. The non-specific test flags any input-dependent difference, including leakage of public data such as ciphertexts, so for lattice-based PQC (ML-KEM/ML-DSA) a failing result does not by itself show that a secret leaks. Labs therefore add specific tests on the stages that handle secrets: NTT/INTT transform, polynomial multiplication, and modular reduction. |t| > 4.5 (the common threshold from Goodwill et al., 2011) indicates statistically significant leakage.

definition: A compatibility mapping showing which combinations of client and server PQC algorithm configurations successfully negotiate a shared secret. Used during the lab testing phase of PQC migration to identify which vendor combinations are compatible, require fallback, or are incompatible.
technicalNote: Key findings from production interop testing: Chrome 130+ (hybrid X25519+ML-KEM-768) is compatible with Cloudflare, AWS, and OQS test servers. Pure PQC clients (no classical component) are rejected by Cloudflare's server policy. Legacy TLS 1.2 servers reject all PQC ClientHello extensions — connection succeeds via fallback but PQC is not used. Use test.openquantumsafe.org for reference server testing.

definition: A comprehensive catalog of all cryptographic assets across an organization — including algorithms in use, key sizes, certificate types, library versions, protocol configurations, and their locations across code, infrastructure, and third-party systems.
technicalNote: Crypto inventory differs from CBOM in scope: CBOM is code-level (source and binaries), while a crypto inventory spans network traffic (passive discovery), endpoint configuration (active scanning), and code analysis. A complete inventory combines all three: passive network probes (CryptoNext COMPASS, pqc-flow) + endpoint scans (pqcscan) + CBOM generation (CBOMkit). Typical enterprise inventory phase: 2–4 weeks for network + 1 week for endpoint scans.

definition: A set of established metrics for classical cryptographic algorithm performance (ECDH, RSA, ECDSA) used as a reference point to measure the overhead introduced by PQC algorithms. Enables data-driven decisions about hardware capacity, latency budgets, and migration sequencing.
technicalNote: Critical baselines for PQC migration: TLS handshake latency (classical: 8ms LAN, 68ms WAN), IKEv2 SA setup (classical: 38ms LAN, 240ms WAN), certificate size (RSA-2048: 1.2KB). PQC overhead vs baseline: hybrid TLS ~1.2x handshake latency, pure-PQC IKEv2 up to 53x SA setup time on WAN. Tools for baseline measurement: PQC-LEO (open source), VIAVI TeraVM (commercial), Keysight CyPerf (freemium).

definition: A set of negotiated cryptographic algorithms (encryption, integrity, PRF) agreed upon between two network peers.
A random cryptographic value (typically 32 bytes) sent by the Initiator (Ni) or Responder (Nr) to prevent replay attacks and contribute to key derivation.

RFC 8554 stateful hash-based signature scheme that composes multiple LMS trees into a single signing capability with extended lifetime. PQC-relevant for firmware / software signing where the key state can be tracked.

Cryptographic primitive that produces a ciphertext encapsulating a fresh shared secret under the recipient's public key. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is the NIST-standardised PQC KEM; classical examples include RSA-KEM and DHKEM.

Cryptographic function that derives one or more secret keys from a shared secret, password, or master key. PQC handshakes use HKDF (RFC 5869) to expand the KEM-output shared secret into traffic keys and resumption keys.

Framework of policies, processes, and components that issues, distributes, validates, and revokes digital certificates. PQC migration of PKI requires new certificate, CRL/OCSP, and timestamp signature algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA).

A signature design that proves knowledge of a secret by simulating what a multi-party computation would output, then revealing just enough of the simulation to be verifiable. Used by FAEST (AES-based), MQOM (multivariate quadratic), and SDitH (syndrome decoding).
technicalNote: MPCitH signatures are typically kilobytes — larger than lattice or multivariate — but security reduces to well-studied symmetric or combinatorial assumptions rather than newer algebraic structures.

definition: PQC algorithms built on the hardness of finding isogenies (structure-preserving maps) between supersingular elliptic curves. Offers the smallest combined public key + signature sizes of any PQC family. SQIsign is the leading on-ramp candidate.
technicalNote: The earlier isogeny KEM SIKE was broken in 2022 by the Castryck–Decru attack. SQIsign uses a different mathematical structure that avoids the same exploit, but the field is young and conservative deployments treat it with caution.

definition: PQC algorithms based on the hardness of solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations (usually quadratic) over a finite field. Produces tiny signatures and large public keys. Candidates include UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA.
technicalNote: The 2025 Ran wedge attack hit several UOV / MAYO / SNOVA parameter sets. Reparameterisation to odd-characteristic fields restores security; QR-UOV was unscathed.

definition: NIST's ongoing process for additional post-quantum signature algorithms beyond the schemes it selected earlier (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, FN-DSA). Progress is documented in NIST IR 8528 (first round, October 2024) and NIST IR 8610 (second round, May 2026); the aim is to diversify the signature portfolio, with particular interest in schemes that do not use structured lattices.
technicalNote: NIST advanced nine candidates to the third round in May 2026: MPC-in-the-Head (FAEST, MQOM, SDitH), multivariate (UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA), isogeny (SQIsign) and lattice (HAWK). The HAWK team withdrew it on 29 July 2026, leaving eight candidates and none that is lattice-based. NIST expects the third round to last about two years.

definition: The continuous, iterative management discipline of knowing what cryptography you have, keeping it healthy, and proving it across certificates, libraries, application software, and key material. Distinct from crypto-agility (capability) and from a CryptoCOE (operating model).
technicalNote: CPM is organised around five pillars (Inventory, Governance, Lifecycle, Observability, Assurance) and a six-stage operational loop (Discover → Classify → Score → Remediate → Attest → Reassess) wrapped in a strategic annual PDCA cycle.

definition: The provisioning, rotation, revocation, and retirement workflow for X.509 certificates across an enterprise. Becomes mathematically impossible to run manually under CA/B Forum SC-081v3's 47-day TLS cert validity (March 2029).
technicalNote: Modern CLM is driven by ACME (RFC 8555), EST (RFC 7030), and CMP (RFC 4210). Shadow-cert discovery via Certificate Transparency logs is a standard input. Forrester TEI 2025 modelled 312% ROI on CLM automation for one vendor — treat as upper bound.

definition: An organisational operating model that centralises ownership of cryptography across an enterprise — answering 'who owns it?' for crypto-agility (capability) and CPM (program).
technicalNote: This module's ROI model assumes about 50% lower PQC transition cost for organisations with a CryptoCOE in place before 2028; it is an illustrative assumption, not a sourced figure. The CryptoCOE typically owns standards, exception handling, KMS / HSM platform decisions, and library / vendor approvals.

definition: The cost of the best known classical attack on an algorithm, measured in equivalent brute-force operations — not the key length. RSA-2048 reaches only ~112 bits because the General Number Field Sieve (GNFS) factors large numbers sub-exponentially. ECC P-256 reaches ~128 bits because Pollard's rho is fully exponential, costing exactly k/2 bits where k is the key size. Under Shor's algorithm on a quantum computer, both reach 0 — all classical asymmetric algorithms are fully broken regardless of key size.
technicalNote: Source: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 2 (RSA-2048 = 112 bits). Quantum resource estimates: Gidney & Ekerå 2021 (RSA) and Roetteler et al. 2017 (ECC).

definition: The SLH-DSA hypertree has d layers of XMSS trees, each of height h/d. The lowest layer signs FORS public keys; higher layers sign the roots of XMSS trees below them. The SLH-DSA public key contains both the public seed PK.seed and the top root PK.root.
technicalNote: FIPS 205 specifies complete parameter sets: -f variants favor signing speed and -s variants favor smaller signatures. The layer count is one parameter in that trade-off; changing it alone does not establish the security of a new parameter set.

definition: PKCS#11 attribute controlling whether a private or secret key may be wrapped. CKA_EXTRACTABLE=CK_FALSE prevents C_WrapKey export; CKA_SENSITIVE separately restricts reading protected key material with C_GetAttributeValue.
technicalNote: CKA_WRAP_WITH_TRUSTED adds a restriction on which wrapping keys may be used; it does not override CKA_EXTRACTABLE=CK_FALSE. A separate vendor backup interface has its own rules and must not be inferred from C_WrapKey policy.

definition: PKCS#11 key attribute that, when CK_TRUE, prevents a key's value from being revealed by C_GetAttributeValue — the token refuses to disclose the raw secret.
technicalNote: Combined with CKA_EXTRACTABLE=CK_FALSE to give a key that can be used but never read out.

definition: PKCS#11 attribute marking an object as persistent on the token (CK_TRUE) versus a temporary session object (CK_FALSE) that disappears when the session closes.
PKCS#11 function that generates an asymmetric key pair (public + private) directly inside the token, so the private key can be created non-extractable and never exists outside the HSM.
PKCS#11 function that encrypts (wraps) one key with another so it can be exported or backed up as ciphertext — e.g. AES key-wrap of a data key under a key-encryption key.
technicalNote: The wrapped key's CKA_EXTRACTABLE must be CK_TRUE for C_WrapKey to succeed.

definition: PKCS#11 v3.2 function for KEM encapsulation: given a recipient's public key it produces a ciphertext plus a freshly derived shared-secret key object — used for ML-KEM (FIPS 203).
PKCS#11 mechanism for AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394) — deterministic, authenticated wrapping of key material under an AES key-encryption key, with an integrity check value.
technicalNote: CKM_AES_KWP (RFC 5649) is the padded variant for wrapping keys whose length is not a multiple of 8 bytes.

definition: A Cooperative Patent Classification symbol (e.g. H04L9/0852) that categorizes a patent by subject matter. Jointly developed and maintained by the USPTO and the European Patent Office, CPC codes are hierarchical — sections (letters) subdivide into classes, subclasses, groups, and subgroups, with longer codes indicating more specific technology.
technicalNote: The USPTO replaced its own classification system (USPC) with CPC on January 1, 2013. A single patent typically carries several CPC codes.

definition: The earliest date an inventor can claim to have disclosed an invention, typically from an earlier-filed provisional or foreign application. It is the date patent examiners use to judge whether the claimed invention is novel against prior art.
technicalNote: The priority date often equals the filing date, but not always — a later non-provisional filing can claim priority back to an earlier provisional.

definition: The date a complete patent application was formally submitted to the patent office. It anchors the start of prosecution and (for the earliest non-provisional filing in a family) the patent term calculation.

The date a patent is formally granted and becomes enforceable — sometimes called the grant date. It marks the end of examination, when the patentee gains the legal right to exclude others from the claimed invention.

A patent claim that stands alone and defines the invention completely without referring to any other claim. Every patent has at least one. Independent claims set the broadest scope of protection; dependent claims narrow an independent claim by adding further limitations and must be read together with it.

In the EU Digital Identity Wallet architecture, the general term for an attestation from the Wallet Provider that describes the components of a wallet unit. Its two subtypes are the Wallet Instance Attestation (the wallet app instance) and the Key Attestation (the secure keystore). A PID Provider is required to verify the wallet's WIA and KA, and check that neither is revoked, before issuing a PID.
An attestation of attributes issued by a Qualified Trust Service Provider, carrying legal weight across all EU member states.

term: Public Body Electronic Attestation of Attributes
definition: An attestation issued by a public body on the basis of an authentic source.
Cryptographic proof that the entity presenting a credential controls the private key the credential was bound to at issuance.
The secure hardware storing an EUDI wallet's private keys. Can be local (device secure element, eSE, TEE) or remote (cloud HSM).
The firmware or software managing cryptographic operations inside the WSCD.
Standard API for remote signature creation services, used by QTSPs for remote qualified electronic signatures. Version V2.2 was published in November 2025.
Privacy property ensuring that multiple presentations by the same credential holder cannot be correlated across different Relying Parties.
The GDPR principle (Article 5(1)(c)) requiring collection of only the personal data necessary for a specific purpose. Selective disclosure enforces it cryptographically rather than by policy.
A machine-readable registry of Qualified Trust Service Providers published by each EU member state, enabling cross-border trust verification.
The cross-border mechanism ensuring mutual recognition of digital identities, wallets and qualified attestations across all 27 EU member states.
A Hardware Security Module operated by a provider rather than held on the user's device. The EUDI ARF supports both local WSCD and remote WSCD (HSM) models.

The CBOR-encoded mobile document credential format defined by ISO/IEC 18013-5, carrying a Mobile Security Object signed as a COSE_Sign1 structure. Optimised for proximity presentation over NFC or BLE.
The Selective Disclosure JWT Verifiable Credential profile (draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc), built on base SD-JWT (RFC 9901). Uses the dc+sd-jwt media type, which replaced vc+sd-jwt in November 2024.
A CBOR Object Signing and Encryption single-signer signature structure (RFC 9052), used by ISO 18013-5 mdocs to sign the Mobile Security Object.
The protocol used to query and update directory services such as Microsoft Active Directory — the store of user accounts, groups, and credentials that authentication systems rely on.
technicalNote: LDAP channels are typically secured with StartTLS or LDAPS (LDAP over TLS), so LDAP's own PQC exposure is really the TLS layer beneath it: the handshake needs hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, and any client-certificate authentication needs an ML-DSA-capable CA chain. LDAP simple binds that send credentials in the clear (no TLS) remain a separate, non-quantum risk.

definition: The most widely deployed open-source cryptography and TLS toolkit, providing both a command-line tool and the libssl/libcrypto libraries that a large share of Linux, network appliance, and application-layer software links against for TLS and general cryptographic operations.
technicalNote: OpenSSL 3.5 (April 2025) added ML-KEM and ML-DSA to its default provider, so any application linked against system OpenSSL 3.5+ gains hybrid PQC TLS support without code changes — the same mechanism the oqsprovider add-on supplied for older 3.x releases. Distinct from OpenSSL Provider, which is the plugin architecture that makes this pluggable.

definition: The organisational function that measures, reports on, and governs risk — as distinct from a SOC, which detects and responds to it. GRC produces the instruments a board uses for oversight, a CISO uses to manage a program, and internal audit uses to verify it.
technicalNote: For a PQC migration, GRC is what turns a cryptographic inventory (a CBOM) into board-level risk reporting, tracks migration milestones against regulatory deadlines, and provides the audit trail that a program actually happened rather than merely being claimed.

definition: A filtering layer, typically deployed alongside a reverse proxy or CDN edge node, that inspects HTTP(S) requests for application-layer attacks (SQL injection, XSS, and similar) before they reach an origin server.
technicalNote: Because a WAF sits inline with TLS traffic — often terminating it itself — its PQC readiness follows the same path as any other TLS termination point: the underlying TLS stack needs hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, and certificate validation needs to tolerate the larger ML-DSA certificate chains.

definition: A directive issued by the U.S. President to federal agencies, carrying the force of law without requiring Congressional approval. Executive Order 14412, "Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks" (June 22, 2026), is the order currently driving federal PQC migration deadlines.
technicalNote: EO 14144 (January 2025) first added PQC provisions to federal cybersecurity policy; EO 14306 (June 2025) narrowed them. EO 14412 superseded both, setting concrete deadlines (FIPS 203/ML-KEM key establishment by Dec 31 2030, FIPS 204/ML-DSA signatures by Dec 31 2031 for High Value Assets) and is implemented via OMB Memorandum M-26-15.

definition: A standardized identifier system for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities, maintained by MITRE with CISA sponsorship, so a single CVE ID can be cross-referenced across advisories, scanners, and databases like the NVD.

A machine-readable statement, typically paired with an SBOM, declaring whether a product is actually affected by a specific known vulnerability (CVE) — cutting down alert fatigue from CVEs that exist in a dependency but aren't reachable or exploitable in that product.

A signature format that combines a post-quantum signature (e.g. ML-DSA) with a traditional signature (e.g. ECDSA or Ed25519) into one value that verifies as a unit. A well-constructed composite stays unforgeable as long as at least one component does, but what that protects against depends on which component is broken and on the attacker (classical or quantum).
technicalNote: Distinct from a Composite Certificate, which is the X.509 container that can carry a composite signature. Specified in the IETF LAMPS working group's composite ML-DSA Internet-Draft. It gives no backward compatibility: only upgraded verifiers understand its algorithm identifiers.

definition: A fault-tolerant unit of quantum information built from many physical qubits combined via quantum error correction. Estimates of when a quantum computer could break RSA or ECC are expressed in logical qubits, not physical ones.

A single physical two-level quantum system (e.g. a trapped ion, superconducting circuit, or photon) used as a qubit before error correction. Many physical qubits — current estimates range from hundreds to well over a thousand, depending on the error-correction code — are needed to form one reliable logical qubit.

An active implementation attack that deliberately induces a physical fault — voltage or clock glitching, laser pulses, electromagnetic pulses — during a cryptographic operation to force an incorrect computation and leak secret material.
technicalNote: Distinct from a Side-Channel Attack, which passively observes normal operation rather than disturbing it.

definition: A milestone at which a quantum computer performs a specific computation infeasible for any classical computer in a practical time, regardless of whether that computation is useful.
technicalNote: Largely superseded in current usage by the more application-relevant term Quantum Advantage, also in this glossary.

definition: The CMVP process for validating an entropy source — the combination of a noise source, health tests and an optional conditioning component that produces random bitstrings for a random bit generator — against NIST SP 800-90B. An accredited laboratory tests the entropy source and submits it through NIST's Entropy Source Validation Test System (ESVTS), and a validated entropy source may be referenced by certificate number in multiple modules without being recertified.
technicalNote: Source: NIST SP 800-90B (January 2018), Section 3 'Entropy Source Validation' (p. 9) and Glossary (p. 62); NIST CMVP Entropy Validation Announcements page, 'ESV Program Rollout' of April 13, 2022 and 'Entropy Source Validation Test Server' of March 24, 2022 (page footer 'Updated August 21, 2026'); NIST ESV-Server README (usnistgov/ESV-Server). SP 800-90B states that validation provides additional assurance that adequate entropy is provided by the source. ESVTS runs the SP 800-90B Entropy Assessment Library to analyze entropy sources, and its Prod environment is available to NVLAP-accredited labs with the 17ESV accreditation scope.

definition: A kind of cryptographic algorithm self-test in which a module operates an algorithm on a set of known input vectors and compares the result to the known expected output; if the calculated output does not equal the known answer, the self-test fails. The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance calls it the most common way to meet an algorithm self-test requirement, alongside comparison tests and fault-detection tests.
technicalNote: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 10.3.A (pp. 102-103, quoting ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.2) and General Notes 6-7 (p. 115). General Note 7 permits a KAT to verify equality by comparing a hash of the calculated output to a hash of the known expected output; that hash function must itself be self-tested first. For ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA the guidance describes KATs that use fixed, predetermined values (pp. 110-112).

definition: A conditional self-test that a FIPS 140-3 cryptographic module performs on the cryptographic functions of each approved algorithm it implements, before the algorithm's first operational use. A CAST may take the form of a known-answer test, a comparison test or a fault-detection test.
technicalNote: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 10.3.A 'Cryptographic Algorithm Self-Test Requirements' (pp. 102-103, quoting ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Sections 7.10.3.1 and 7.10.3.2) and General Notes 5 and 8 (p. 115). Unless otherwise stated, CASTs are performed on the algorithms and parameters (for example key sizes, curves, modes) that an approved service uses. The requirement also applies to allowed algorithms with a claim of security and to legacy algorithms, but a CAST is not required before first execution in the non-approved mode.

definition: A conditional self-test that a cryptographic module must perform on every public and private key pair it generates; the Implementation Guidance treats it as separate from a cryptographic algorithm self-test. For ML-KEM key pairs it consists of encapsulating a shared secret with the encapsulation key and decapsulating the result with the decapsulation key, and it passes if the two shared secrets are equal. It is not required when a key or key pair is imported from outside the module's cryptographic boundary.
technicalNote: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 10.3.A (p. 103, quoting ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3) and its Additional Comment 1 (pp. 115-116). For key pairs generated for SP 800-208 (LMS, XMSS) or FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), the PCT may be limited to confirming that the resulting public and private key share the same key identifier.

definition: In FIPS 140-3, the term that covers both critical security parameters (CSPs) and public security parameters (PSPs). For example, an AES-GCM initialization vector is considered an SSP (a PSP or a CSP) within the module validation, and SSP establishment is the process by which CSPs or PSPs are securely shared within a module or between two or more entities.
technicalNote: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG D.A 'Acceptable SSP Establishment Protocols' (p. 176), IG D.B 'Strength of SSP Establishment Methods' (p. 178) and IG C.H Additional Comment 10 (p. 155). FIPS 140-3 and NIST SP 800-140B Rev. 1 use the term (SP 800-140B expands the abbreviation) but do not define it.

definition: The vendor-provided, non-proprietary document that the CMVP requires for a cryptographic module; its required content comes from ISO/IEC 19790 Annex B and ISO/IEC 24759 Section 6.14 as modified by NIST SP 800-140B. Its sections follow the Annex B order, from 'General' to 'Mitigation of other attacks', and any section that does not apply is marked as such. Among other things it records the module's cryptographic boundary, the approved modes of operation and how each is configured, and a table of the module's sensitive security parameters.
technicalNote: Source: NIST SP 800-140B Rev. 1, CMVP Security Policy Requirements (November 2023), Abstract (p. i), 'Security Requirements' (pp. 3-5) and section 2.4 (p. 9); FIPS 140-3 (March 22, 2019), section 3.3. For example, the vendor-provided non-proprietary security policy must list all vendor-affirmed security methods (p. 5).

definition: The explicitly defined perimeter that establishes the boundary of all components — the set of hardware, software or firmware components — of a cryptographic module. FIPS 140-3 test requirements have the tester verify that the module's block diagram indicates this boundary, and the module's security policy must define it precisely and list any hardware, software or firmware excluded from it.
technicalNote: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 9.5.A (p. 85) and IG 2.3.B (p. 27), both quoting the ISO/IEC 19790:2012 definition; NIST SP 800-140 (March 2020), assertions AS02.15, AS02.17 and AS02.18 (pp. 3-5); NIST SP 800-140B Rev. 1 (November 2023), pp. 7 and 9. The test requirements set the boundary rule separately for hardware, firmware and hybrid modules; a hybrid module's boundary is the composite of its hardware component boundary and the disjoint software or firmware component boundary.

definition: In Common Criteria, an implementation-independent statement of security needs for a type of target of evaluation (TOE). It describes the TOE type and the security functional and assurance requirements expected of it, and is typically written where a user community, a regulator or a group of developers wants to define a common set of security needs. A Security Target for a specific product may conform to one or more Protection Profiles.
technicalNote: Source: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and general model (CC:2022 Revision 1, November 2022), clause 3.68 (p. 22), 5.2.2.3 (p. 30), 6.3.3.2 (p. 39) and Annex B.2.1 (p. 125). Clause 10.1 (p. 66) says a PP is intended to describe a general TOE type, so it may be used as a Security Target template for any TOE of that type.

definition: In Common Criteria, an implementation-dependent statement of security requirements for a specific target of evaluation (TOE), based on a security problem definition. It is a document that describes the TOE, the conformance claims, the security problem, the security objectives and the security requirements, and it is typically produced by the developer. It may conform to one or more Protection Profiles.
technicalNote: Source: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and general model (CC:2022 Revision 1, November 2022), clause 3.82 (p. 24), 5.2.2.3 (p. 30), 12.1 (p. 89) and Annex D.2.1 (p. 149). Before and during the evaluation the ST specifies what is to be evaluated; after the evaluation it specifies what was evaluated.

definition: In Common Criteria, the set of software, firmware and/or hardware, possibly accompanied by guidance, that is the subject of an evaluation. A TOE may be an IT product, a part of an IT product, a set of IT products, a unique technology that can never be made into a product, or a combination of these, and the Security Target must outline its physical and logical scope.
technicalNote: Source: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and general model (CC:2022 Revision 1, November 2022), clause 3.90 (p. 25) and clauses 5.3.1-5.3.2 (p. 33). The CC says the relation between the TOE and any IT product matters in one respect: the evaluation of a TOE containing only part of an IT product should not be misrepresented as the evaluation of the entire IT product.

definition: The CMVP list of cryptographic modules on which the CMVP is actively working. For each submission it shows the module name, vendor name, standard and status together with the date the module went into that status. Because validation is a joint effort of the CMVP, the laboratory and the vendor, the list gives some indication of which of them has the action. Participation is voluntary, the list does not necessarily include all modules being tested or reviewed, and posting on it does not imply or guarantee FIPS 140 validation.
technicalNote: Source: NIST CMVP Modules In Process List page (csrc.nist.gov), 'Last Updated: 10/3/2026'; FIPS 140-3 CMVP Management Manual, Version 2.7 (April 9, 2026), section 4.2 (p. 31) for the voluntary-participation and no-guarantee statements. Per the page, a module moves from Pending Review to Review only after the lab pays the NIST Cost Recovery fee. Status values shown include Pending Review, Review, Comment Resolution - Lab, Comment Resolution - CMVP, Pending Resubmission, Cost Recovery and Finalization; the page does not describe each state and points to the CMVP Modules In Process page for details.

definition: An independent, NVLAP-accredited laboratory (also written 'CST lab') that tests cryptographic modules for the CMVP. It tests a module to the FIPS 140-3 requirements for the security level and embodiment, and produces a written test report for the CMVP Validation Authorities, who review it. Vendors submit a module and its documentation to the accredited CSTL of their choice.
technicalNote: Source: FIPS 140-3 CMVP Management Manual, Version 2.7 (April 9, 2026), sections 1.1 (p. 1), 2.6.1-2.6.2 (p. 13) and 2.6.3 (p. 15). A CSTL can conduct algorithmic testing and verify compliance with the algorithm standards (there may be additional requirements beyond what is CAVP-tested), review the module's documentation and source code, and perform the required testing in accordance with the test requirements, SP 800-140x and the Implementation Guidance.
